chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from his father, from Abdullah ibn Bukayr, from Zurara, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

Samura ibn Jundab had a tree in the garden of a man from the Ansar, and the house of the Ansari was at the gate of the garden, and he used to pass by it to his palm tree and did not seek permission. So the Ansari spoke to him that he should seek permission when he came, but Samura refused. When he refused, the Ansari went to the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) and complained to him and informed him of the news. So the Messenger of Allah sent a messenger to him and informed him of what the Ansari said and what he complained about, and said: 'If you intend to enter, seek permission.' But he refused. When he refused, he bargained with him until he reached the price that Allah willed, but he refused to sell it. He said: 'For you is a tree extended to you in Paradise,' but he refused to accept. So the Messenger of Allah said to the Ansari: 'Go and uproot it and throw it at him, for there is no harm and no causing harm.'

key_terms.الْأَنْصَارِيُّ: The man from the Ansar (Helpers of Medina)
key_terms.حَائِطٌ: A garden or enclosed plot of land
key_terms.سَاوَمَهُ: He bargained with him / negotiated the price
key_terms.عَذْقٌ: A single tree or a small cluster of trees
key_terms.لَا ضَرَرَ وَ لَا ضِرَارَ: No harm and no causing harm (a fundamental legal maxim)

ai.seo_question: What is the legal principle of 'no harm' (la darara wa la dirar) in Islamic jurisprudence regarding property disputes?
ai.summary: In this narrative from *Al-Kafi*, the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) resolves a property dispute between Samura ibn Jundab and an Ansari man, illustrating the practical application of the principle 'la darara wa la dirar' (no harm and no causing harm). The resolution involves a unique legal mechanism where the Prophet instructs the aggrieved party to uproot the offending tree and throw it at the owner, thereby transferring ownership and eliminating the source of harm. This incident is frequently cited by Shia jurists to demonstrate that the removal of harm can take various forms beyond simple compensation, emphasizing the flexibility of Islamic jurisprudence in maintaining social harmony.
